strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea: the observation that verifying multi-view 3D consistency is far more tractable than generating it makes RL with a verifiable reward a natural fit for 3D scene editing, and the paper is (to my knowledge) the first to apply GRPO-based RL to 3D editing, bypassing the scarcity of paired 3D-consistent editing data.

Interesting and well-supported core technical insight: the empirical analysis of VGGT's confidence maps (Fig. 5, with a quantitative near-linear correlation between consistency degradation and average confidence) provides a convincing justification for using a 3D foundation model as a geometry-aware verifier, going beyond hand-crafted consistency measures.

Thoughtful reward design addressing known RL failure modes: the anchor reward with offline single-view edits explicitly prevents the reward-hacking toward over-smoothed/low-frequency outputs, and ablations comparing against SfM-based and reprojection-warping rewards (Tab. 2, Fig. 7) convincingly demonstrate that traditional verifiers are easily hacked, validating the necessity of data-driven priors.

Strong experimental evidence for the claims: best performance across all four evaluation dimensions (Tab. 1), large quality margin over the strongest re-implemented FLUX-based baseline (VIEScore 5.48 vs. 3.23), ~2-20x faster inference, ablations of each reward component, transferability to Qwen-Image-Edit, and demonstrated zero-shot generalization to unseen instructions and scenes.

Fair-comparison effort: re-implementing the strongest baseline (EditSplat) under the same FLUX-Kontext backbone, using identical prompts and camera poses, and pioneering VIEScore for reproducible 3D editing evaluation. Honest limitations section on backbone context-length constraints and training scale.
weaknesses: Limited training and evaluation scale relative to the generalization claims: training uses only 8 scenes and 70 prompts (1,319 samples), and the zero-shot claims rest on only 30 additional test cases (16 unseen instructions, 14 new scenes). While the authors acknowledge this, the breadth of generalization (arbitrary scenes/instructions) is asserted more than demonstrated, and behavior on out-of-distribution scene types (e.g., large outdoor/urban environments, reflective or thin structures) is not shown.

Baseline comparison is somewhat confounded: most compared methods (DGE, GaussCtrl, EditSplat) use the weaker InstructPix2Pix backbone, so the large VIEScore gap partly reflects the backbone upgrade rather than the RL framework alone; only one FLUX-based re-implementation (EditSplat) is provided, and no comparison against Tinker despite it also using FLUX-Kontext.

Evaluation relies heavily on VLM-based metrics: VIEScore (GPT-4.1) drives the headline claim, CLIP-dir differences are small (0.147 vs. 0.125), and Ph-Loss differences are marginal (0.076 vs. 0.077 for GaussCtrl); the user study is deferred to the appendix, so the perceptual quality advantage is not independently verified in the main paper. The consistency of VIEScore ratings across methods should be sanity-checked.

Ablations are conducted only on face scenes with ~200 samples; conclusions about reward components and alternative verifiers are drawn from a narrow data regime, and it is not fully established that the findings transfer to the full training setup.

Citation hygiene problems undermine scholarly rigor: reference [48] attributed to VGGT is actually a completely unrelated paper ('Statistical characteristics of the proton isotropy boundary'), references [17]/[18] and [14]/[15] are duplicated, and several entries carry implausible future dates/arXiv IDs (e.g., [39], [60], [64]). These errors need correction and suggest insufficient care in the bibliography, though they do not affect the technical contribution.

Some methodological details are underspecified in the main text: the reward weighting (all 0.25) is presented without sensitivity analysis, the effect of the 12-step vs. 6-step exploration is only asserted, and potential failure modes of VGGT confidence as a reward (e.g., whether blurriness or novel appearance styles systematically depress confidence and bias the model) are only partially discussed.

strengths: The core idea is interesting and timely: using RL (GRPO) to inject 3D-consistency priors into a strong 2D editor (FLUX-Kontext), sidestepping the scarcity of 3D-consistent paired editing data. Framing 'verifying consistency is easier than generating it' as the RL motivation is well argued.

The insight that a frozen 3D foundation model (VGGT) can serve as a consistency verifier is a genuinely novel contribution, and the empirical analysis in Fig. 5 (progressive view replacement showing near-linear confidence decay) provides a reasonable validation of the premise.

The ablation study is comparatively thorough for the method's core design: it ablates each reward component and directly compares alternative verifiers (SfM-based reward, reprojection warping reward), including concrete demonstrations of reward hacking (textureless outputs for SfM, blurry outputs for warping), which strengthens the case for the VGGT-based reward.

The anchor reward mechanism, using offline single-view FLUX-Kontext edits as quality anchors, is a sensible design to prevent RL degradation of the 2D editing prior, supported by both ablation (Table 2) and a 2D-capability check (Fig. 3).

The paper honestly discusses limitations (backbone sequence-length trade-off, limited training scale), and reports training/inference efficiency transparently. Comparisons include a re-implementation of the strongest baseline under the same FLUX-Kontext backbone, which is fair-minded.
Zero-shot generalization to unseen instructions and scenes is demonstrated qualitatively, and transferability to a second editing backbone (Qwen-Image-Edit) is shown quantitatively.
weaknesses: Serious attribution and citation integrity problems: the reference for VGGT (the paper's central dependency, [48]) points to an unrelated proton-physics paper (arXiv:2409.04488). Multiple references are duplicated verbatim ([17]/[18], [37]/[38], [45]/[46], [14]/[15]), and several citations carry impossible future dates/IDs (e.g., arXiv 2602.11638, 2602.09432, 'MixGRPO (2026)'). While these may be clerical, they undermine confidence in the manuscript's overall care and in proper credit assignment.

The evaluation scale is small and potentially fragile: only 8 training scenes with ~70 prompts and ~1,300 training samples, and 100 total test cases (70 in-distribution). Claims of 'SoTA' quality and generalization rest on a very narrow data footprint, and all ablations are trained and tested only on face scenes, limiting the generality of the design conclusions.

The primary quantitative metric is VIEScore, a GPT-4.1-based VLM judge, and the reported margin (5.48 vs. 3.23, a ~70% leap) is suspiciously large. The user study is deferred to the appendix and absent from the main text; for a heavily perceptual task like scene editing, main-paper human evaluation is important, and VLM-judge sensitivity to sharpness/fidelity could inflate the comparison against optimization-based methods that produce blurrier renders.

The reward design has an unaddressed bias risk: VGGT's confidence reflects both multi-view consistency and in-distribution plausibility. The Fig. 5 analysis itself shows that valid localized edits (glasses) reduce confidence, suggesting the reward may penalize out-of-distribution content and push the model toward conservative, identity-preserving edits. The claimed robustness to reward hacking is argued more than rigorously demonstrated for the VGGT reward itself.

The fairness of the headline comparison is partially compromised: the strongest prior FLUX-based method (Tinker) is discussed but not empirically compared, and most baselines rely on a demonstrably weaker InstructPix2Pix backbone. The comparison against the authors' own re-implementation of EditSplat w/ FLUX (which takes 40 min) is helpful but not equivalent to a well-tuned original method.

Several claims are under-supported or vague: 'extensive experiments' vs. an 8-scene training set; 'verifying 3D consistency is tractable' is asserted without quantifying verifier reliability (e.g., false-positive consistency rates); and key statements like 'we think it can optimize consistency while preserving high-quality output' are hedged rather than evidenced. Section 3.4 is titled 'Overview of Reward Model' but contains full method details, hurting organization.

The contribution is primarily an application of existing components (Flow-GRPO, MixGRPO, LoRA fine-tuning, VGGT, FLUX-Kontext); the novelty, while real, is in the combination and reward design, so the modest scale of evaluation matters more than it would for a deeper methodological contribution.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated paradigm: the paper clearly articulates the asymmetry between generating and verifying multi-view consistency, and convincingly positions RL as a natural fit for 3D editing. To the authors' knowledge (and mine), this is the first application of RL to 3D scene editing, which is a meaningful conceptual contribution.

The identification of VGGT as a 3D consistency verifier is insightful. The empirical analysis (Fig. 5) showing near-linear decay of VGGT confidence with progressive consistency degradation provides a credible basis for using it as a reward, and the ablations (r^SfM, r^warp) demonstrate that data-prior-based verification better avoids reward hacking than classical geometric rewards.

The anchor reward design (Eq. 3) is a sensible mechanism for preserving 2D editing fidelity while enforcing 3D consistency, and Fig. 3 plus the VIEScore evaluation on GEditBench-EN provide evidence that RL fine-tuning does not degrade the backbone's 2D editing capability.

Strong empirical results: large quantitative gains (VIEScore 5.48 vs 3.23), lowest Ph-Loss, 1.5-minute editing time (>2x faster than prior pipelines), a fair re-implementation of the strongest baseline (EditSplat w/ FLUX-Kontext) under the same backbone, and zero-shot generalization to unseen instructions/scenes.
Honest limitations section (backbone token-length trade-off, GRPO training cost) and a promise to release code and models, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited training scale and generalization evidence: training uses only 8 scenes and 1,319 samples for one epoch, and the zero-shot evaluation covers just 14 new scenes and 16 new instructions. Given only 8 training scenes, there is a risk of overfitting to scene statistics; a broader evaluation across scene categories would materially strengthen the claims of generalization.

Heavy reliance on VIEScore (GPT-4.1) as the primary quality metric; the reported gap (5.48 vs 3.23) is unusually large for a VLM-judge metric and single-metric dependence introduces evaluation risk. The user study is deferred entirely to the appendix and not summarized in the main text, so the reader cannot assess human preference evidence at face value. No 3DGS reconstruction quality metrics (e.g., novel-view FID/PSNR of the edited 3D scene) are reported.

Potential circularity: the reward is VGGT confidence, and the main consistency metric reported alongside quality (Ph-Loss) is computed with VGGT-predicted depth/GT poses. There is a risk the optimized model is tuned toward VGGT's confidence structure rather than true geometric consistency; independent consistency verification (e.g., multi-view stereo or epipolar checks computed without VGGT) would help rule this out.

The anchor reward effectively injects FLUX-Kontext's offline single-view outputs as pseudo-references, making the method partially a form of self-distillation rather than purely 'RL without supervision'; the paper's framing ('bypassing the scarcity of paired data') slightly overstates the supervision-free nature.
Ablations are restricted to face scenes with ~200 samples, which may not generalize conclusions about reward components to diverse scenes.

Attribution and reference-quality issues: reference [48], cited throughout as VGGT, is actually a proton physics paper (incorrect attribution of a central prior work); references [17]/[18] and [37]/[38], [45]/[46], [14]/[15] are duplicated. These should be corrected as they affect scholarly accuracy.

The 1.5-minute editing-time comparison is somewhat favorable by construction: RL3DEdit is a single-pass multi-view editor while baselines perform per-scene optimization; the comparison with Tinker (the other FLUX-based, non-per-scene method mentioned in related work) is missing from the quantitative table.

The paper does not discuss how robust the VGGT-confidence reward is to adversarial 'reward hacking' over long training horizons, only that it empirically outperformed two alternative verifiers; a longer-term stability analysis or failure-case discussion would strengthen the core claim.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated contribution: the paper convincingly argues that verifying 3D consistency is more tractable than generating it, positioning RL (GRPO) with a 3D foundation model (VGGT) as the verifier. To the authors' knowledge this is the first application of RL to 3D scene editing, and the idea is cleanly mapped onto the reward model paradigm.

The empirical analysis in Fig. 5 is a genuine strength: the near-linear correlation between consistency degradation and VGGT confidence, with per-region effects (background vs. foreground vs. object replacement), provides interpretable evidence that VGGT confidence is a meaningful reward signal rather than an arbitrary proxy.

Comprehensive and well-designed ablations: reward components (r^D, r^P, r^T, r^a), alternative verifiers (SfM, photometric warping) with clear reward-hacking demonstrations, backbone transfer (Qwen-Image-Edit), denoising steps, anchor selection, and reward weights all substantiate the design choices.

Fair baseline treatment: the authors re-implement the strongest baseline (EditSplat) under the same FLUX-Kontext backbone, and additionally show that prior methods rely on per-scene optimization while their method is single-pass — the 1.5 min editing time with zero-shot generalization to unseen scenes and instructions is a substantial practical advantage.

Thorough supplementary material (GRPO details, reward definitions, dataset construction with full instruction lists, per-split metrics, user study with 25 participants, failure cases) supports reproducibility, and the authors commit to releasing code and models.
Honest limitations section: attention-sequence-length trade-offs, structural deformation failures, and the computational cost of GRPO are candidly discussed rather than hidden.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on VLM-based evaluation (VIEScore with GPT-4.1) as the headline metric. The reported gap (5.48 vs. 3.23) is very large, and because RL3DEdit preserves FLUX-Kontext's output distribution, VLM judges may systematically favor FLUX-style generations over baselines trained on InstructPix2Pix, inflating the apparent improvement. Quantitative evidence beyond VIEScore and CLIP-dir (e.g., LPIPS/PSNR/SSIM against pseudo-GT where available, or 3D metrics like depth agreement) would strengthen the case. The user study mitigates but does not remove this concern.

Small-scale training and evaluation: 8 scenes, 70 training prompts, and 100 test cases is a limited benchmark for claims of generalization and SoTA. The 30 zero-shot cases are sparse, and the ablations are confined to face scenes; the authors acknowledge the scale limitation, but conclusions about generalization would benefit from broader scene diversity.

The anchor reward depends on pre-computed single-view FLUX-Kontext edits, which are themselves 3D-inconsistent. This effectively biases all views toward matching one view's edit semantics; cases where the correct edit differs across views (view-dependent content, occlusion boundaries) are not analyzed in depth.

Potential circularity in verifier selection: VGGT confidence is validated on synthetic degradation experiments (replacing views), but its behavior under realistic edited-content distributions (stylized edits, structural changes) is less characterized; the SfM/warping baselines shown to be hackable are relatively easy targets, and robustness of the chosen reward over long RL training (drift, residual hacking modes) is not studied.

Some evaluation-metric fairness caveats: Ph-Loss differences against GaussCtrl are small (0.076 vs. 0.077), yet the paper claims best consistency; and efficiency comparisons mix very different backbones (InstructPix2Pix-based pipelines at minutes vs. FLUX-based pipelines), making the headline speedup partly an artifact of backbone choice rather than method design.

Minor editorial issues: several references are duplicated with inconsistent numbering (e.g., [21]/[22], [46]/[47], [57]/[58]), and a few citations carry implausibly future-dated venues, which slightly undermines polish and should be corrected.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated framing: the observation that verifying 3D consistency is more tractable than generating it naturally casts the problem as RL with a verifiable reward, and to my knowledge this is the first application of RL (GRPO) to 3D scene editing.

The empirical analysis of VGGT (Fig. 5, Sec. 3.3), showing near-linear decay of confidence with consistency degradation, is a convincing and useful piece of evidence that a 3D foundation model can serve as a consistency verifier.

The anchor reward is a thoughtful design choice: it preserves the 2D editor's fidelity (validated by Fig. 3 showing VIEScore drop <1% on GEdit-Bench) while the geometric rewards enforce multi-view consistency, addressing the classic trade-off that causes reward hacking.

The ablations are unusually thorough and honest: ablating each reward, and especially the comparison against SfM-based and reprojection-warping rewards, concretely demonstrates reward hacking (textureless/blurry outputs) and justifies the data-driven verifier. Supplementary ablations (anchor selection, denoising steps, reward weights) add rigor.

Strong practical results: single-pass inference (~1.5 min vs 3.5–40 min baselines), lowest Ph-Loss, and zero-shot generalization to unseen instructions/scenes, with a user study (25 participants) in the appendix.

Limitations are discussed candidly (backbone token-capacity limits, large non-rigid deformations, small training scale), and the method transfers to Qwen-Image-Edit, suggesting the framework is not backbone-specific.
weaknesses: A critical baseline is missing: vanilla FLUX-Kontext multi-image joint editing of the 9 views *without* RL. Since the headline gains (VIEScore 5.48 vs 3.23) partly reflect the much stronger 2D backbone (FLUX-Kontext vs InstructPix2Pix used by all baselines), the paper needs to isolate the contribution of RL itself. EditSplat w/ FLUX-Kontext partially addresses this but uses a different mechanism (MFG guidance); a direct 'base editor, no RL' row in Tables 1/2 is needed to substantiate the central claim that RL is the key ingredient.

Heavy reliance on VIEScore (a GPT-4.1-based VLM metric) as the primary quality measure, with an unusually large jump over all baselines; the main-paper quantitative evidence would be more convincing with a larger user study or additional objective 3D-consistency metrics beyond Ph-Loss. VLM-based scores can be gamed by plausible-looking but geometrically inconsistent renders.

The VGGT confidence reward verifies *geometric* consistency but not semantic/instruction consistency across views: the anchor covers only one randomly chosen view, so whether all M views faithfully realize the same instruction magnitude (e.g., 'open mouth — how wide?') is enforced only implicitly through the base model. The paper's own motivating example is thus only partially resolved by the reward design.

Training and evaluation scale is small: 8 scenes and 70 prompts for training; zero-shot generalization is tested on only 4 new scenes and 14 instructions. Claims of broad generalization are therefore supported only in a narrow regime, and the near-perfect in-distribution results may partly reflect the limited diversity of test scenes.

The confidence-consistency analysis (Fig. 5⑥) is based on a simple view-replacement protocol on 100 sets; it does not probe whether VGGT confidence can itself be reward-hacked over the course of full RL training (Fig. S2 is suggestive but anecdotal). A longitudinal analysis of the reward distribution during training would strengthen the robustness claim.

Presentation sloppiness: duplicated bibliography entries (refs 21/22, 46/47, 57/58), inconsistent citation details, and a raw LaTeX label visible in Eq. 1's caption area suggest the manuscript was not carefully proofread; these do not affect the science but reduce confidence in overall care.

Per-scene baselines are given per-scene optimization on test data while RL3DEdit is amortized, which the authors acknowledge; still, the in-distribution (70 novel-view) comparison conflates backbone strength with method advantage, as noted above.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea: reframing multi-view consistency as a verification problem amenable to RL, and being the first (to the authors' knowledge) to apply RL/GRPO to 3D editing. The 'generate is hard, verify is tractable' asymmetry argument is compelling and clearly articulated.

Empirically grounded reward design: the empirical analysis in Fig. 5 (confidence decaying near-linearly with progressive view replacement over 100 sets of 9-view data) provides reasonable evidence that VGGT confidence is a valid consistency proxy, and the ablation (Tab. 2 ④⑤, Fig. 7, Fig. S2) convincingly demonstrates that SfM-based and photometric-warping rewards are reward-hackable while VGGT is more robust.

Comprehensive experimental evidence: quantitative comparison (Tab. 1) with re-implemented strongest baseline (EditSplat under FLUX-Kontext), per-split in-distribution vs zero-shot results, a user study (25 participants), qualitative comparisons across diverse editing types (motion, replacement, style, background, addition), and multiple ablations (rewards, anchor strategy, denoising steps, reward weights, backbone transfer to Qwen-Image-Edit).

Efficiency and data-efficiency gains: single-pass inference (~1.5 min, 2x faster than pipelines and 20x faster than the FLUX-based baseline) trained on only ~1.3K samples / 8 scenes, with demonstrated zero-shot generalization to unseen instructions and scenes.

Good methodological care: anchor reward design preserves 2D editing fidelity (validated in Fig. 3 via VIEScore on GEditBench showing <1% drop), KL regularization to the reference policy, honest limitations section covering backbone token-length constraints, large non-rigid deformations, and training scale.
Fair-comparison efforts and release commitment: re-implementing EditSplat with the same backbone, consistent prompts/camera poses, and stated intent to release code and model improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity and metric weakness: VIEScore (GPT-4.1) is the primary quality metric and is a relatively noisy, VLM-based proxy; Ph-Loss relies on VGGT-predicted depth, the same model used as the reward signal, raising a mild train/eval coupling concern. No standard perceptual metrics (e.g., FID/KID on novel views) or dedicated consistency measures independent of VGGT.

Limited training and evaluation scale: training uses only 8 scenes and 70 prompts; the test set is 100 cases with 25-participant user study. While zero-shot results mitigate this, conclusions about generality across scene types (outdoor/indoor variety, reflective/transparency materials) remain under-supported.

Potential reward-hacking of VGGT itself is only argued, not exhaustively ruled out: the paper shows VGGT penalizes blurry/textureless outputs (Fig. S2), but systematic stress tests (e.g., adversarial probing of the reward over long training, style-heavy cases where confidence may behave unpredictably) are limited; the authors themselves note lower performance on stylized edits without quantifying it.

Heavy dependence on the anchor strategy: preservation of editing fidelity leans on offline single-view FLUX-Kontext edits with 'light quality filtering' (>98% usable is an empirical, unverified claim); failure modes when single-view edits are wrong (e.g., misinterpreted instructions) propagate uncorrected into all views, and this failure mode is not analyzed.

Fixed inference setup: M=9 views with GT camera parameters for 3DGS reconstruction; handling fewer views requires duplication and more views is left to future work, limiting applicability to real captures with irregular view counts/poses. The claimed robustness of VGGT rewards to viewpoint changes is not stressed under pose noise.

Presentation issues: duplicated bibliography entries (refs 21/22, 46/47, 57/58), several references with implausible future years (2026 arXiv IDs), LaTeX artifacts visible in equations (raw \label, \frac commands in the parsed text of Sec. 3.4), and Fig. 2 is dense and hard to parse; these do not undermine the science but indicate incomplete polishing.

Some comparisons may favor the method structurally: prior baselines are per-scene optimization methods evaluated at their paradigm's strengths, whereas RL3DEdit is a generalist model; the VIEScore gap (5.48 vs 3.23) is large and would benefit from more granular per-category analysis (the split exists in the appendix but per-instruction-type breakdown is not reported).
